questions.q: What is a microservice?
questions.explain: A microservice runs as its own process, is deployed on its own, and owns its own data. A folder with one feature inside one app is a module of a modular monolith, not a service.
options: A folder inside one application that holds one feature
A small application that owns one business area and runs as its own process, usually with its own database
A function that is called over the network instead of directly
A shared database that several applications read and write

questions.q: On a sale day the catalog gets a hundred times more reads than payments. Which microservice benefit helps here?
questions.explain: With separate services you can run twenty catalog servers and only two payment servers. Independent deployment is about releasing on your own schedule, which is a different benefit.
options: Independent deployment
Independent scaling
Fault isolation
One shared database transaction

questions.q: In the modular monolith, catalog.reserve() was a function call. After you extract catalog into a service, what new problem does that call have?
questions.explain: A function call in one process cannot time out. A network call can be slow, fail, never answer, or be delivered twice. Most of the lesson is about making that call as reliable as the function call was.
options: It can no longer return a value
It must be written in a different language
It becomes a network call that is much slower and can fail, hang or arrive twice
It can only be called once per day

questions.q: You are starting a new online shop and do not yet know where the business boundaries are. What does the lesson recommend?
questions.explain: Moving a boundary between two services is far harder than moving it between two folders. A modular monolith lets you find the right boundaries first; you extract a service when independent deployment or scaling is a measured need, not a guess.
options: Start with microservices so you never have to split later
Build a modular monolith first, and extract a module into a service when a reason is real and measured
Build one big file and split it when it gets slow
Start with one service per database table

questions.q: The orders service needs a product's price. The catalog service owns the products table. What should orders do?
questions.explain: A service owns its data: no other service reads its tables. Reading them directly ties both services to one table layout and bypasses catalog's rules. Ask through the API, or keep a copy fed by events.
options: Connect to the catalog database and read the products table directly
Copy the catalog database password into its own config
Ask the catalog service through its API, or keep its own copy updated from catalog's events
Ask the user to type the price in the order form

questions.q: In Docker Compose, why does http://catalog:3000 reach the catalog service?
questions.explain: Docker Compose and Kubernetes give every service a DNS name. You need a registry such as Consul only at a scale where configuration plus DNS names stop working.
options: Because catalog is a special word in HTTP
The platform's DNS answers the name catalog with the right address, even when containers move
Because every service listens on the same IP address
Because a service registry like Consul is always included

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: url.host includes the port, so it is catalog:3000 (hostname would be just catalog). The payments value is set, but its protocol is ftp:, so the second check throws.
options:
catalog:3000

catalog

questions.q: The environment variable is set to an empty string. What does this print?
questions.explain: An empty string is falsy, so !raw is true and the function throws its own clear message before new URL ever runs. Treating empty the same as missing is what you want for required config.
options: http://localhost/
CATALOG_URL is not set
Invalid URL
undefined

questions.q: After checkout, ShopFlow sends a receipt e-mail. The customer does not wait for it. Which way of talking fits best?
questions.explain: Use synchronous calls only when a user is waiting for the answer. A queue lets orders hand the work over and finish, and a slow mail provider cannot slow down or fail the checkout.
options: A synchronous HTTP call from orders to the e-mail service
A synchronous RPC call with a long timeout
A job on a queue, processed later with retries
Writing into the e-mail service's database directly

questions.q: In the example, inventory takes 2 seconds to answer for a lamp, and the client has timeout: 1000. Why is the timeout important?
questions.explain: Without a timeout, every waiting request keeps memory and a connection busy in orders. A slow dependency can then make orders itself fall over. Give every remote call a timeout.
options: It makes inventory answer faster
Orders stops waiting after one second and answers its caller with a clear 503
It retries the lamp request forever until it works
It cancels the order in the database

questions.q: A POST /charges request timed out. Why is it dangerous to simply send it again?
questions.explain: The server may have finished the work and only the answer was lost. Retrying a read is harmless, but retrying "charge this card" could charge twice, unless you use an idempotency key.
options: Timeouts never happen twice
The caller cannot know whether the server did the work, so a retry could charge the card twice
A timeout always means the server is down forever
The server rejects every second request

questions.q: The client sent x-request-id: req-mug, orders passed it on, and inventory logged it. Why is this useful?
questions.explain: A correlation id ties together log lines from different services. It is not a security token: it proves nothing about who sent the request.
options: It makes the request faster
It encrypts the request between services
It is a correlation id: you can search every service's logs for one id and see the whole story of one request
It proves the request came from a logged-in user

questions.q: The lesson checks an id from an incoming header before copying it into logs. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only letters, digits, _ and - up to 64 characters pass. The second value contains a newline and spaces, so it is replaced; otherwise an attacker could write a fake line into your logs.
options:
req-mug
gen-2
gen-3

req-mug
bad
gen-3

req-mug
gen-2
undefined

gen-1
gen-2
gen-3

questions.q: Why does HttpClient add a random jitter to each backoff wait?
questions.explain: Without jitter, every client retries on the same schedule and hits the recovering service in waves. A little randomness spreads the retries out.
options: To make tests less predictable
So a thousand clients that failed at the same moment do not all retry at the same moment too
To hide the real delay from attackers
Because timers in Node.js are not exact

questions.q: What does this exponential backoff schedule print?
questions.explain: Each wait doubles: 100, 200, 400, 800. Math.min(…, max) caps them at 300, like maxRetryDelay in the lesson's client.

questions.q: How does an idempotency key make "charge this card" safe to retry?
questions.explain: The key names the operation, not the attempt. The first attempt did the work; the retry with the same key gets the saved answer, so the card is charged once.
options: The server charges again but refunds the first charge
The caller sends the same unique key with every attempt; the server saves the answer per key and returns the saved answer when the key comes again
The server rejects every second request from the same IP
The caller waits longer before retrying

questions.q: The first attempt charged the card but its answer was lost. What does this print?
questions.explain: The second call finds the saved answer for key-1 and replays it with replayed: true. The charge counter is not increased again.
options:
{ chargeId: 1, replayed: true }
cards charged: 1

{ chargeId: 2, replayed: false }
cards charged: 2

{ chargeId: 1, replayed: false }
cards charged: 1

{ chargeId: 2, replayed: true }
cards charged: 2

questions.q: In production, where should the payments service keep the saved answers for idempotency keys?
questions.explain: A Map is lost on restart and is not shared between instances. Saving the answer in the same transaction as the charge means you can never have a charge without its saved answer.
options: In a Map in memory, forever
In the caller's browser
In the database (or Redis) with an expiry, saved in the same transaction as the charge
In a log file that is read on every request

questions.q: A circuit breaker is open. What happens to a call?
questions.explain: Open means "fail fast": no more load on a service that is already struggling, and no caller waits for a timeout. After the pause the breaker goes half-open and lets one trial call through.
options: It is sent to the service and retried three times
It fails at once without touching the network, until the pause is over and one trial call is allowed
It waits in a queue until the service is back
It is sent to a different random service

questions.q: A breaker opens after 2 failures in a row. What does this print?
questions.explain: The second failure opens the breaker. The third call fails fast even though the service is up, because the breaker does not touch the network while it is open.
options: 503, 503, failing fast | open
503, 503, ok | closed
503, failing fast, failing fast | open
503, 503, ok | open

questions.q: The breaker around inventory is open. Which page can safely show "stock unknown" as a fallback?
questions.explain: A product page can live without the stock count. Checkout cannot accept an order it cannot reserve, so there the right answer is a clear "please try again in a minute".
options: Checkout, because the order can be fixed later
The product page, which can still show the product and sell it
The payment page, which can charge now and check stock later
No page, fallbacks are never safe

questions.q: A receipt job fails on all of its attempts. What happens to it in the queue?
questions.explain: The dead-letter list keeps failed jobs visible instead of losing them. Because a job may run more than once, its handler should be idempotent too.
options: It is deleted silently
It is retried forever
It moves to the dead-letter list, where a person can look at it
The checkout that created it is rolled back

questions.q: Why does the lesson tell you to avoid two-phase commit (2PC) between services?
questions.explain: 2PC tries to lock both databases and commit them together. The outbox and saga patterns give you consistency without that coupling.
options: It is not allowed by the HTTP standard
It is slow, needs every service up at the same time, and most modern databases and brokers do not support it across systems
It only works with MongoDB
It sends every event twice

questions.q: The orders service saves the order, then publishes order.placed, and crashes between the two. How does the outbox pattern fix this?
questions.explain: Both rows are saved or neither is, so an order can never exist without its event. The relay then reads unpublished rows, publishes them and sets published_at.
options: It publishes the event before saving the order
It writes the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the order; a relay publishes it later and marks it published
It retries the crash until it succeeds
It stores the event in memory until the next restart

questions.q: The relay crashes after publishing an event but before marking it published. What does the receiving service need?
questions.explain: The outbox gives at-least-once delivery: the unmarked event is sent again on the next run. At-least-once plus idempotent handlers is the normal, reliable combination.
options: Nothing, the event will never arrive twice
A distributed transaction with the relay
An idempotent handler that ignores duplicates, for example by remembering handled orderIds
A longer timeout

questions.q: This simulates the outbox relay. What does it print?
questions.explain: Each run publishes only rows that are not yet published, then marks them. The new row is sent on the second run, and the third run finds nothing left.
options:
relayed: 2
relayed: 1
relayed: 0

relayed: 2
relayed: 3
relayed: 3

relayed: 2
relayed: 0
relayed: 0

relayed: 2
relayed: 1
relayed: 1

questions.q: The same event is delivered twice. What does this print?
questions.explain: Order 7 is handled once (10 − 2 = 8), its duplicate is skipped, and order 8 takes one more: 7. Without the handled set the stock would wrongly drop to 5.
options: stock: 7
stock: 5
stock: 8
stock: 10

questions.q: In a saga, what is a compensation?
questions.explain: A saga does not roll back like a database. When a step fails, it runs the compensations of the steps that already succeeded, moving forward to a consistent state like "order cancelled, stock released".
options: A database rollback across two services
An action that undoes a finished step, such as releasing reserved stock
A retry of the failed step
A payment to the customer for waiting

questions.q: The third step fails. What does this saga print?
questions.explain: Only finished steps are undone, and in reverse order: the stock was reserved last, so it is released first. The failed step did nothing, so it has nothing to undo.
options:
undone: reserve stock
undone: create order
confirmed: false

undone: create order
undone: reserve stock
confirmed: false

undone: charge card
undone: reserve stock
undone: create order
confirmed: false

undone: reserve stock
undone: create order
confirmed: true

questions.q: What is the difference between an orchestrated and a choreographed saga?
questions.explain: Orchestration has a conductor, which is easier to follow when you start. Choreography has none: order.created → inventory reserves → stock.reserved → payments charges, and so on.
options: Orchestrated sagas use HTTP, choreographed sagas use SQL
In an orchestrated saga one service tells the others what to do; in a choreographed saga each service reacts to the previous service's event
Choreographed sagas cannot undo steps
Orchestrated sagas run all steps at the same time

questions.q: What does the W3C traceparent header carry from one service to the next?
questions.explain: With those two ids, the receiving service starts its span as a child of the caller's span in the same trace, so a tracing tool can draw one timeline across both services.
options: The user's password hash
The full log output of the caller
The trace id and the id of the span that made the call
The response body of the previous request

questions.q: This is a simple check of the traceparent shape. What does it print?
questions.explain: The parts are version, trace id (32 hex), parent span id (16 hex) and flags. The second group is the span id. A header that does not match gives undefined.
options:
097763d1485c4cd3
undefined

cb48117a31190094f0093378c0bcab43
undefined

null

questions.q: Finish shouldRetry(method, status). It returns true only for GET, HEAD and PUT requests that failed with 429, 502, 503 or 504. The program should print true false true false.
questions.explain: Two sets make the rule clear: the method must be idempotent and the status must be one that may go away. A 404 never changes, and a POST could create something twice.

questions.q: Finish backoff(base, retries, max). It returns an array of waits that double each time, starting at base, capped at max. The program should print [ 100, 200, 400, 500, 500 ].
questions.explain: Attempt i waits base * 2 ** i. Math.min stops the wait from growing past the cap, so a long outage does not make clients wait minutes.

questions.q: Finish charge(key, amount) so a retry with the same key does not charge again. Save each answer in answers; when the key was seen before, return the saved answer. The program should print 1 1 2 and then charges: 2.
questions.explain: Look up the key first. Only a new key does the work and saves its answer. The retry with k1 gets the same chargeId, so the card is charged once.

questions.q: The outbox delivers at least once. Finish the order.placed handler so it reduces stock only the first time it sees an orderId. The program should print stock: 8.
questions.explain: Check the set before doing the work, and add the id when you do it. In a real service the set is a table with a unique order_id, written in the same transaction as the stock change.

questions.q: Finish call(work) for a tiny circuit breaker. When open is true, return "stock unknown" without running work. Otherwise run work(): on success reset failures to 0 and return its result; on an error add 1 to failures, set open = true once there are 2 failures, and return "stock unknown". The program should print stock unknown, stock unknown, stock unknown and work ran: 2.
questions.explain: The third call never touches inventory, because the breaker opened after two failures. That is the point: fail fast, and show a fallback where the page can live with it.
questions.expected:
stock unknown, stock unknown, stock unknown
work ran: 2

questions.q: Finish runSaga(steps). Run each step's run() in order. If one throws, call compensate() on the steps that already finished, in reverse order, and return false. Return true if all steps worked. The program should print release stock, cancel order, result: false.
questions.explain: Remember only the steps that finished. The failed charge did nothing, so there is no refund; the others are undone newest first.
questions.expected:
release stock
cancel order
result: false

questions.q: Finish correlationId(incoming, fallback). Return incoming only when it is 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, _ or -; otherwise return fallback. The program should print req-42 gen-1 gen-2.
questions.explain: A header comes from outside, so check its format before you copy it into logs. \w matches letters, digits and _; the anchors ^ and $ make the whole value match.

questions.q: Finish serviceUrl(env, name). Throw `${name} is not set` when the value is missing or empty. Parse it with new URL, and throw `${name} must be an http(s) URL` unless the protocol is http: or https:. Return the URL. The program should print the three lines shown in the starter's comment.
questions.explain: Check configuration at startup, so a missing or wrong address stops the service with a clear message instead of failing on the first customer request.
questions.expected:
catalog:3000
PAYMENTS_URL is not set
MAIL_URL must be an http(s) URL

questions.q: Finish relay(). Publish every outbox row whose publishedAt is null, in order, by calling publish(row), then set its publishedAt to "now". Return how many rows you published. The program should print sent order.placed 1, sent order.placed 3, relayed: 2, relayed: 0.
questions.explain: Publish first, then mark. If the relay crashed between the two, the row would be sent again next time: that is at-least-once delivery, which is why receivers must ignore duplicates.
questions.expected:
sent order.placed 1
sent order.placed 3
relayed: 2
relayed: 0

questions.q: The breaker opens after 2 failures and pauses for 5000 ms. What does this print?
questions.explain: At t=2 the breaker is open, so it fails fast even though inventory is up. At t=6000 the pause is over and one trial call goes through, but it fails, so the breaker opens again at once. At t=6001 it is still inside the new pause.
